rv.q: But still, this is a warm, exuberant ensemble piece full of heart and hope — an absolute tonic.
And, on the whole, it works beautifully.
The result is as grating as it is delightful.
The show gradually weaves a charming spell of its own and mostly steers just the right side of whimsy.
This is perfect Rice territory. No blandness. Beaming warmth. Both homespun and ingenious.
It's very inventive and community-minded – but plotless. Long on charm, short on yarn.
But like many alternative therapies, it felt pleasantly indulgent.
Bagdad Cafe asks us to trust it, to close our eyes and open our palms – but, more often than not, we come up empty-handed.

Rice's version of Bagdad Cafe loses that crucial sense of place, and her adherence to the atmospheric, dialogue-light film gives us a tale that's more bewildering than enigmatic, with underdeveloped characters and undercooked drama.
It's all very charming and full of light humour, but it only flies when the actors burst into song.

What hasn't yet been achieved in this Old Vic premiere is much narrative heft to go with the abundant heart of an evening that ends with a collective Zoom, a reminder in our fraught times of the collective call-out to community.
But despite its heart being manifestly in the right place — definitely, nay defiantly, on its sleeve — the whole thing winds up being considerably less than the sum of its parts.
All in all, Bagdad Café is a wonderful expression of how much we need others in our lives, and it’s fitting that it forms part of the Old Vic’s reopening season.
